pages.headline: Grow the firm without betting it on the hiring market.
pages.outcome: Your growth plan currently has one engine: hire senior people fast enough to keep up with the work you win. Governed AI adds a second engine. Assembly, drafting, retrieval, and synthesis move onto rails, senior attention returns to winning and standing behind work, and revenue can move faster than headcount without the firm's name paying for it.
triggers: The growth plan assumes senior hires the market will not supply at a price the model affords.
Partners are at capacity while the pipeline is still growing, and the choice reads as decline work or dilute quality.
The firm's distinctive expertise is concentrated in a few heads, and succession is a hope rather than a plan.
Clients have started asking how the firm uses AI, and the current answer is individual improvisation.

evidence.text: Enterprise surveys in 2025 find regular AI use near nine in ten organizations, while only a minority report enterprise-level earnings impact and most experiments never fully scale.
evidence.source: McKinsey State of AI 2025; Deloitte generative-AI survey 2025
evidence.caveat: Self-reported, large-enterprise-skewed consultancy surveys. The pattern is about value capture, not professional-services ROI; it argues for operating discipline, not for urgency theater.

pages.headline: More delivery through the same organization, without the wheels coming off.
pages.outcome: You already know where the friction is: work recreated because nobody can find the original, handoffs that lose what was promised, status assembled by hand every week, staffing decided by hallway memory. Governed AI takes the assembly load out of delivery operations while your review gates and escalation paths stay exactly where you put them.
triggers: Utilization looks healthy while delivery still runs late, which means the hours are going somewhere unproductive.
The same proposals, frameworks, and reports keep being rebuilt from scratch across practices.
Staffing scrambles happen through personal networks while qualified people sit unseen on other teams.
The weekly operating picture consumes a day of senior time to assemble and is stale on arrival.

evidence.text: In a field experiment with 758 consultants at one elite firm, AI use on tasks inside its capability frontier meant 12.2 percent more tasks completed, 25.1 percent faster, at more than 40 percent higher judged quality than the control group.
evidence.caveat: Task-level results at one elite firm; not proof for mid-market firms or firm-level margin. The same study found quality damage when AI was used outside the frontier, which is what the review gates are for.

A client asked how the practice uses AI on their work, and the answer depended on who they asked.

evidence.caveat: Which tasks sit outside the frontier shifts with the model and the domain. Accountable human review remains a standing professional requirement, independent of average productivity gains.

pages.headline: One governed platform, instead of thirty ungoverned tools.
pages.outcome: The business is already using AI, approved or not. The question on your desk is whether that becomes a platform you can operate and defend, or a sprawl you get blamed for. Governed AI operations gives you the architecture: engagement-scoped access, approved sources, traceability by default, and a sanctioned path good enough that people stop wanting the shadow one.
triggers: Shadow AI is already in the building: individual subscriptions, browser tools, and nobody can say what client data has touched them.
Practice groups are procuring point tools independently, each with its own data posture and none with a shared control model.
Client security questionnaires have started asking AI questions the current estate cannot answer cleanly.
Leadership wants AI rolled out and IT is expected to make it safe after the fact.

evidence.text: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (January 2023) and its Generative AI Profile (July 2024) give a voluntary, vendor-neutral scaffold for governing AI design, deployment, use, and evaluation.
evidence.caveat: Voluntary frameworks, not mandates and not a professional-liability safe harbor. They have to be adapted to the firm's own duty-of-care and client obligations.

pages.headline: AI use your firm could explain to its most demanding client.
pages.outcome: The risk is not that the firm uses AI. It is that the firm cannot say how, where, or under what controls. Governed AI operations replaces improvisation with a defensible posture: engagement boundaries, human accountability at every consequential point, evidence that reconstructs what happened, and a disclosure answer ready before anyone asks.
triggers: Client contracts have started speaking to AI directly, and the firm's posture varies by whoever is asked.
A near-miss surfaced: client material in an unapproved tool, caught by luck rather than by design.
Professional accountability for AI-assisted work has never been written down, and reviewers are assuming someone else checked.
An insurer, auditor, or client questionnaire asked about AI controls and the answer was assembled overnight.

evidence.text: Quality risk from misapplied AI is not hypothetical: causal field evidence shows professional performance degrades when AI is relied on for tasks outside its capability frontier.
evidence.caveat: Frontier boundaries move as models and domains change. The control implication is task routing and accountable review, not prohibition; prohibition just relocates the risk to shadow tools.

pages.headline: An AI investment case that would survive your own diligence.
pages.outcome: You have seen the vendor math: day-one payback, hours saved that nobody redeployed, benefits counted three times. The governed version is different by construction: baselines before pilots, program cost counted once, adoption lag priced in, ranges instead of points, and freed capacity named to a destination so it lands in margin instead of evaporating.
triggers: AI spend is accumulating across practices with no consolidated view of cost, let alone return.
A vendor business case reached the executive table and did not survive ten minutes of questions.
Margin compression that utilization alone no longer explains, while delivery hours hide recreated work.
The next planning cycle needs an AI line item and there is no defensible number to put on it.

aiChanges: The cost side consolidates: one program cost, counted once, with each workflow carrying only its marginal cost.

evidence.text: Professionals surveyed in 2024 predicted AI would save them about four hours per week in the near term and twelve within five years. Those figures are expectations respondents reported, not observed savings.
evidence.caveat: Vendor-sponsored global survey of predictions. Predicted hours may never convert to utilization, realization, or margin; only a baseline and honest measurement can show whether they do.
